concepts.name: Doctrine of Paramountcy and its Application to Sindh and Punjab
key_dimensions: Definition and legal basis of Paramountcy in British Indian policy
How Paramountcy was used to justify interference in Sindh (Amirs) and Punjab (Sikh Kingdom)
Distinction between Paramountcy and outright annexation as policy tools
Comparison with later application under Lord Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse

concepts.name: Treaty of Lahore (1806) and Early Anglo-Sikh Relations
key_dimensions: Context of Ranjit Singh's rise and British neutrality policy east of Sutlej
Terms establishing the Sutlej as boundary and British non-interference
Why this treaty represented a period of British restraint vs. later aggression
Contrast with the post-Ranjit Singh deterioration of Anglo-Sikh relations

concepts.name: Treaty of Amritsar (1809): Ranjit Singh and the British
key_dimensions: Key terms: Ranjit Singh confined west of Sutlej, British protected the Cis-Sutlej states
Strategic British motivation — containing Napoleonic threat via Persia-Afghanistan
Role of Charles Metcalfe as negotiator and its diplomatic significance
Long-term impact: created a buffer and delayed Sikh-British conflict by decades

concepts.name: Lord Ellenborough's Policy and the Conquest of Sindh (1843)
key_dimensions: Ellenborough's aggressive forward policy and strategic motivations (trade, river access, Afghanistan fallout)
Role of the Indus as a commercial and military highway — Treaty of 1832 and subsequent pressure
Distinction between Ellenborough's approach and the earlier more cautious Sindh policy
Criticism of the conquest as unjustified even by British contemporary opinion

concepts.name: Charles Napier and the Battle of Miani (1843)
key_dimensions: Military context: Napier's campaign against the Talpur Amirs of Sindh
Battle of Miani (February 1843) and Battle of Hyderabad (March 1843) — sequence and outcomes
Napier's alleged dispatch 'Peccavi' — historical myth vs. reality and its UPSC trap potential
Consequences: Sindh formally annexed, Napier appointed its first Governor

concepts.name: The Talpur Amirs of Sindh: Political Structure and British Manipulation
key_dimensions: The Talpur ruling structure — division among Hyderabad, Mirpur, and Khairpur branches
How British exploited internal divisions among the Amirs
Successive unequal treaties imposed on Amirs (1832, 1838, 1839) as a pattern of coercion
Comparison with treatment of other Indian princes under British subsidiary alliance

concepts.name: Critique of the Conquest of Sindh: Contemporary and Historical Debate
key_dimensions: Sir Henry Lawrence and other British officers' moral objections to the annexation
Outram's role — initially critical ('Bayard of India') but still executed the campaign
How the conquest was rationalized through 'civilizing mission' and strategic necessity
UPSC angle: Distinguishing between those who criticized the policy vs. those who executed it

concepts.name: Ranjit Singh's Empire: Structure, Strengths, and Vulnerabilities
key_dimensions: Administrative and military modernization — role of European officers (Allard, Ventura, Court, Avitabile)
The Khalsa Army (Fauj-i-Ain) as a disciplined modern force
Structural weakness: lack of a clear succession system leading to post-1839 instability
Economic base, territorial extent, and why the empire was a formidable but ultimately fragile entity

concepts.name: Post-Ranjit Singh Succession Crisis and Political Instability (1839–1845)
key_dimensions: Rapid succession of rulers: Kharak Singh, Nau Nihal Singh, Sher Singh — causes of instability
Role of the Dogra chiefs (Dhian Singh, Gulab Singh) in court intrigues
Power of the Khalsa Army Panchayats (soldier councils) and their political assertiveness
How British used this instability to build a case for intervention — UPSC trap on timing

concepts.name: Causes of the First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–46): Immediate and Underlying
key_dimensions: Underlying causes: British expansionism, breakdown of Lahore Darbar, Khalsa army pressure on rulers
Immediate cause: Sikh army's crossing of the Sutlej (December 1845)
Debate on whether British deliberately provoked the Sikhs by troop buildup at Ferozepore
Role of Governor-General Hardinge in escalating tensions

concepts.name: Major Battles of the First Anglo-Sikh War and Military Significance
key_dimensions: Key battles: Mudki, Ferozeshah, Aliwal, Sobraon — sequence and strategic outcomes
Why Ferozeshah was the closest the British came to defeat — significance for UPSC factual questions
Role of treachery: Lal Singh and Tej Singh's alleged betrayal of Sikh positions
Military lessons that shaped British policy in the Second Anglo-Sikh War

concepts.name: Treaty of Lahore (1846) and Treaty of Bhyroval (1846): Terms and Implications
key_dimensions: Treaty of Lahore (March 1846): Key terms — war indemnity, cession of Jalandhar Doab, reduction of Khalsa army
Treaty of Bhyroval (December 1846): British Resident given supervisory control over Lahore Darbar during Duleep Singh's minority
How Bhyroval was more significant than Lahore in establishing de facto British control
UPSC trap: Distinguishing between the two 1846 treaties — terms, parties, and purposes

concepts.name: Treaty of Amritsar (1846) and the Creation of Jammu & Kashmir
key_dimensions: Terms: Gulab Singh purchased Kashmir from British for 75 lakh Nanak Shahi rupees
Why this is a landmark transaction — J&K's modern political identity traces here
British motivation: recovering war indemnity without direct administration of the region
Gulab Singh's role in the First Anglo-Sikh War — rewarded despite Sikh defeat, UPSC irony angle

concepts.name: Causes of the Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848–49): Multan and Hazara Revolts
key_dimensions: Revolt of Mulraj at Multan (April 1848) — murder of Vans Agnew and Anderson as trigger
Revolt of Chattar Singh Attariwala in Hazara — broader Sikh resistance
Dalhousie's deliberate delay in responding — building a pretext for full annexation
How the Second War differed from the First in British strategic intent

concepts.name: Major Battles of the Second Anglo-Sikh War: Chillianwala and Gujrat
key_dimensions: Battle of Chillianwala (January 1849) — British tactical reversal, nearly a Sikh victory
Battle of Gujrat (February 1849) — decisive British victory, use of artillery superiority
Surrender of Sikh army at Rawalpindi (March 1849) — end of organized Sikh resistance
UPSC trap: Chillianwala is often confused with a British defeat — clarifying the nuance

concepts.name: Annexation of Punjab (1849) and Dalhousie's Justification
key_dimensions: Formal proclamation of annexation (March 29, 1849) — Dalhousie's policy vs. Board of Control's initial hesitation
Deposition and exile of Maharaja Duleep Singh — treatment of the minor ruler
The Koh-i-Noor diamond: transfer to Queen Victoria as part of the settlement — factual UPSC favourite
Comparison with Doctrine of Lapse annexations — Punjab was conquered, not lapsed

concepts.name: Board of Administration for Punjab (1849–53): Henry Lawrence vs. John Lawrence
key_dimensions: Structure: Board of three — Henry Lawrence, John Lawrence, Charles Mansel
Policy disagreement: Henry Lawrence favoured conciliation of Sikh chiefs; John Lawrence preferred revenue settlement and firm control
Resolution: Henry Lawrence removed in 1853, John Lawrence became sole Chief Commissioner
Long-term significance: John Lawrence's Punjab model influenced British administration across India

concepts.name: Role of the Subsidiary Alliance System as a Precursor to Conquest
key_dimensions: How Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance was used to weaken both Sindh (partially) and native states generally
Comparison: Sindh Amirs were never formally in Subsidiary Alliance but faced similar coercive treaties
Punjab under Ranjit Singh successfully resisted Subsidiary Alliance — contrast with weaker states
UPSC trap: Distinguishing which states formally accepted Subsidiary Alliance vs. those that were simply coerced

concepts.name: Impact of the Afghan Wars on British Policy Toward Sindh and Punjab
key_dimensions: First Anglo-Afghan War (1839–42) — humiliation drove aggressive forward policy in Sindh
British need for the Indus route and Sindh's geographic significance as supply corridor
Punjab's strategic importance as a buffer state before and after the Afghan debacle
How the 'Great Game' with Russia shaped British urgency in annexing both regions

concepts.name: Sikh Misls and the Historical Context of Sikh Political Power
key_dimensions: The 12 Misls as the pre-Ranjit Singh Sikh confederacy — their role and dissolution
How Ranjit Singh unified the Misls to build a centralized kingdom — political genius angle
Why the Misl tradition of decentralized power resurfaced after Ranjit Singh's death
UPSC angle: Misls as a uniquely Sikh political institution with no parallel in other Indian polities
